01 / OPENING NOTE

What if the thing people say about your brand is the thing that makes it unmistakably yours?

Every brand accumulates a reputation. Some of it is designed. Some of it arrives through habit, culture, jokes, reviews, old advertising, or one sentence someone said online that simply refused to die.

Marketers are trained to correct the unflattering bits. Make the brand look younger. More premium. More sophisticated. More everything.

But sometimes a stereotype is not a crack in the brand. It is the outline of the brand already living in people's heads.

McDonald's found one. Then it stopped fighting it.

A DIFFERENT BRAND QUESTION

Not “How do we change what people think?”

Try “What do people already think that only we can make meaningful?”

02 / THE FLIP

Not for the first date.
For everything after.

McDonald's UAE took a cultural joke about first dates and asked a more interesting question: what if being the wrong place to impress someone is exactly what makes you the right place once the performance is over?

MCDONALD'S UAE × FP7 MCCANN DUBAI
THE OBSERVATION 01

FIRSTDATE.

The place you choose when the first impression matters.

PERCEPTIONROLE
01 / 06
01
THE OBSERVATION

The joke already existed. The brand did not invent the stereotype.

McDonald's UAE and FP7 McCann started with a familiar cultural perception: McDonald's is not the obvious setting when you are trying to make a first impression on a date.

That distinction matters. The insight was not that people suddenly disliked McDonald's. The insight was that the brand already occupied a very specific social role in the mind: easy, familiar, ordinary.

THEY ALREADY HAD THE SHORTHAND
A brand does not always need to create a perception. Sometimes the work begins by noticing the one culture has already handed you.
02
THE MISREAD

“Not impressive enough” was only true for one moment.

First dates are unusually loaded with performance. You are selecting a place, an outfit, a story, even a version of yourself. A restaurant can feel like part of the pitch.

McDonald's everydayness can look like a weakness inside that frame. But step outside the frame and the same quality starts to behave differently. Familiarity is not impressive. Familiarity is comfortable.

SAME ATTRIBUTE / DIFFERENT OCCASION
The strategic opportunity was not to prove the stereotype wrong. It was to change the occasion in which the stereotype was being judged.
03
THE HUMAN TRUTH

Relationships get better when you stop trying to impress.

The deeper truth is less about restaurants and more about relationships. A first date is about possibility. Later dates are about pattern, comfort, inside jokes, ordinary Tuesdays and the places you keep returning to.

That is where McDonald's could become emotionally useful without pretending to be luxurious or romantic. The ordinary place becomes meaningful because the relationship around it has become meaningful.

PERFORMANCE → COMFORT
The brand did not borrow romance from elsewhere. It found a version of intimacy that already fit its everyday identity.
04
THE FLIP

So McDonald's did not deny the joke. It finished it.

The campaign turned the cultural shorthand into the proposition: “Not for the first date. But for every other one.”

That second sentence changes everything. The stereotype stays intact. The context changes. Suddenly, “not first” is no longer the punchline. It becomes the set-up for the brand's actual role.

STEREOTYPE → POSITIONING
This is what makes the idea feel bigger than a witty line. The line gives the stereotype a strategic job.
05
THE EXPANSION

Then the joke became a campaign system.

The idea was not left as one piece of copy. The campaign translated it across billboards, posters, drive-thrus and tray liners, while showing couples across different life stages.

That matters because a stereotype only becomes an asset when it can travel. The idea expanded from one social moment into a repeatable territory for the brand to occupy.

ONE LINE → MANY TOUCHPOINTS
The campaign did not ask audiences to learn a new McDonald's. It asked them to notice a relationship the brand had been part of all along.
06
THE BRAND ROLE

Comfort stopped being a compromise. It became the point.

This is the deeper marketing move. McDonald's did not become more premium, more intimate or more sophisticated. It made its existing role more legible.

The place after the first date is not a product feature. It is an occasion, a memory and eventually a piece of relationship infrastructure. That is how a stereotype can move from “what people say” to “why people choose.”

FAMILIARITY → MEMORY → IDENTITY
The strongest flips do not erase the old association. They make that association useful enough to become part of the brand's identity.

03 / THE DEEPER IDEA

A stereotype is
a shortcut.

Brand image is not a spreadsheet of attributes. It is a network of associations. A stereotype compresses a complicated object into something the mind can retrieve quickly.

The association is not necessarily the problem.
The unowned association is.

You can spend years trying to overwrite a cultural association. Or you can ask whether it contains a truth your competitors cannot credibly claim.

CASUAL FAMILIAR COMFORT UGLY MESSY OLD-FASHIONED
BRANDMEMORY
THE REAL SHIFT

Move from “How do we change what people think?” to “What do people already think that only we can make meaningful?”

The “ugly”
shoe.

The silhouette looked like a liability. Then the brand stopped asking it to be a normal shoe.

THE MOVE / MAKE INDIVIDUALITY THE POINT

They turned being unmistakable into the product.

Crocs leaned into its distinctive silhouette, personalization and collaborations rather than trying to make the clog conventionally unobjectionable.

brand.

The old-fashionedness became theatre.

“Smell Like A Man, Man” exaggerated the brand's masculine heritage into surreal confidence and then made the audience part of the performance.

03 / BURGER KINGFLIP ↗

The “ugly”
burger.

When the category makes food look flawless, showing what real food does becomes a powerful reversal.

THE MOVE / BREAK THE BEAUTY CONVENTION

The decay became the proof.

Moldy Whopper broke the category convention of over-produced burger photography by showing the Whopper rotting across 35 days to signal no preservatives.

05 / THE BRAND MIRROR

People do not carry
strategy decks.

A 2025 mixed-method study examined 100 print ads from 10 brands in five categories in Austria and found brand stereotypes in 91 of those ads.

WHAT THE NUMBER DOES
AND DOES NOT SAY

The study shows that brand-related stereotypes are common in this sample. It does not show that embracing any stereotype automatically creates brand success. The strategic question is whether a recognisable association is also true, ownable and useful.

06 / THE PLAYBOOK

Make the joke
useful.

The move is not to embrace every criticism. It is to find the association that is both recognisable and true, then give it a job inside the brand.

1

Listen before you polish.

Look at jokes, comments, reviews, memes and habits. Cultural perception often arrives before the research deck does.

2

Separate insult from insight.

Not every negative association is useful. The gold is where the stereotype contains a truth the brand can credibly own.

3

Give the stereotype a job.

McDonald's did not simply say “we are casual.” It made casualness mean comfort, familiarity and the freedom to stop performing.

4

Repeat until it becomes memory.

A clever reversal is a campaign. Repeated consistently, it can become a distinctive association people retrieve without prompting.

5

Do not over-explain the joke.

The strongest flips leave enough space for the audience to recognise the truth themselves. Recognition is part of the reward.

OWNERSHIP STACK
SIGNAL → TRUTH → ROLE → REPETITION → MEMORY
07 / A MERCATO BRIEF TAKEAWAY

You do not always need
a new story.

Sometimes you need the courage to finish the old one differently. McDonald's did not make itself more romantic. It made its existing role more meaningful. Crocs did not make the clog conventionally beautiful. Old Spice did not become a different brand overnight. Burger King did not make the Whopper prettier. The most interesting move was deciding what an already-familiar truth should mean.

01

Do not confuse polish with identity.

A smoother perception is not automatically a stronger one.

02

Find the truth inside the joke.

The stereotype is useful when it points toward something real.

03

Own a role, not just a trait.

“Casual” is forgettable. “The place after the first date” is a role.

04

Repeat until it becomes yours.

Distinctiveness grows when the same meaning keeps returning.

THE QUESTION TO LEAVE WITH

Maybe a brand does not become distinctive by escaping what people say about it.

Maybe it becomes distinctive by deciding what that story means.
